candidates.scenario: Personal service — direct delivery to tenant
candidates.facts: Process server personally hands the 3-day notice to the tenant at the rental unit. Tenant accepts the notice.
candidates.question: Is service valid under CCP §1162(a)(1)?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: CCP §1162(a)(1) authorizes personal delivery of the notice to the tenant. Direct hand-delivery is the most preferred method and requires no follow-up mailing.
candidates.edge_cases: If tenant refuses to accept, server should place notice at feet or otherwise effectuate delivery — refusal does not defeat service.

candidates.scenario: Substituted service — left with adult at premises + mailed copy
candidates.facts: Tenant is not home. Process server leaves the notice with tenant's adult roommate (18+) at the premises and mails a copy to tenant at the same address the same day.
candidates.question: Is this valid substituted service under CCP §1162(a)(2)?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: CCP §1162(a)(2) permits substituted service by leaving notice with 'a person of suitable age and discretion' found at the residence, plus mailing a copy to the tenant at the same address. Both elements are satisfied here.
candidates.edge_cases: The adult must be at the premises (not just on the property) and must be of 'suitable age and discretion.' A minor does not qualify.

candidates.scenario: Substituted service — left with minor child
candidates.facts: Tenant is not home. Process server leaves the notice with tenant's 15-year-old child at the door and does not mail a copy.
candidates.question: Is service valid?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: Defect 1: A 15-year-old is not a 'person of suitable age and discretion' under CCP §1162(a)(2). Defect 2: Even if the recipient qualified, substituted service also requires mailing a copy to the tenant — omitted here. Either defect alone voids the service.
candidates.edge_cases: Courts have not set a bright-line age floor for 'suitable age and discretion' below 18, but 15 is generally below the threshold accepted in practice.

candidates.facts: Process server attempts personal service on three separate occasions over two days (morning, afternoon, evening). On the third attempt, tenant is still not home and no one answers. Server posts the notice on the main door and mails a copy to tenant at the premises address.
candidates.question: Is nail-and-mail service valid under CCP §1162(a)(3)?
candidates.DRAFT_answer: YES — valid nail-and-mail if prior attempts were reasonable
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: CCP §1162(a)(3) authorizes posting on the main door plus mailing when (a) personal and substituted service have been attempted without success, and (b) neither the tenant nor a competent person was found at the premises after reasonable attempts. Three attempts at different times of day over multiple days satisfies the 'diligence' requirement. The mailed copy is required — satisfied here.
candidates.edge_cases: Courts examine whether attempts were truly diligent (different days, different times). A single attempt is not sufficient to establish prior failure.

candidates.scenario: Nail-and-mail — no prior personal service attempts
candidates.facts: Without attempting personal service, process server posts the notice on the front door and mails a copy. No attempts at personal or substituted service were made.
candidates.question: Is nail-and-mail valid?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: CCP §1162(a)(3) requires that personal service and substituted service have been attempted and failed before nail-and-mail is permissible. Skipping directly to nail-and-mail without prior attempts voids the service. Losornio v. Motta (1998) 67 Cal.App.4th 110 is directly on point.
candidates.edge_cases: Landlord must prove diligent prior attempts in UD proceeding. If not documented, court will scrutinize.

candidates.scenario: Mail-only service (no personal or substituted attempt)
candidates.facts: Landlord mails the 3-day notice by first-class mail without making any in-person attempt at service.
candidates.question: Is mail-only service valid under CCP §1162?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: CCP §1162 does not authorize mail-only as a standalone service method for residential UD notices. Mail is only used as the follow-up component of substituted service or nail-and-mail. See Losornio v. Motta (1998). Mail-only service is void.
candidates.edge_cases: Note: TX and other states do permit mail service — this is CA-specific. Do not generalize.

candidates.scenario: Nail-and-mail: notice posted but copy not mailed
candidates.facts: Process server posts notice on main door after three failed personal service attempts. Server does NOT mail a copy to the tenant.
candidates.question: Is service valid?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: CCP §1162(a)(3) requires BOTH posting AND mailing for nail-and-mail to be complete. The mailing is a mandatory component, not optional. Omitting the mailed copy voids the service.
candidates.edge_cases: If copy is mailed days after posting, courts may look at when 3-day period begins — but failure to mail at all is a void defect.

candidates.scenario: Substituted service: mailed copy sent to different address
candidates.facts: Process server leaves notice with adult at the premises (123 Main St) but mails copy to tenant's old address (456 Oak Ave, which landlord has on file from an old form), not the rental unit.
candidates.question: Is substituted service valid?
candidates.DRAFT_answer: NO — void (mailed copy to wrong address)
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: CCP §1162(a)(2) requires mailing to the tenant at the place where the notice was left (i.e., the rental premises address). Mailing to a different address does not satisfy the statutory requirement. Service is void.
candidates.edge_cases: If landlord can show tenant actually received the notice despite wrong address, some courts may find actual notice — but statutory compliance is required for a valid UD.

candidates.scenario: Service by certified mail only (no in-person attempt)
candidates.facts: Landlord sends the 3-day notice by certified mail, return receipt requested. Tenant signs for it and receives it.
candidates.question: Is certified mail service valid for residential UD notice in CA?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: CCP §1162 does not recognize certified mail as a standalone authorized service method for residential UD notices, even if the tenant actually receives and signs for it. The three enumerated methods (personal, substituted + mail, nail-and-mail) are exclusive. Actual receipt does not cure a void service method.
candidates.edge_cases: Note: TX expressly permits certified + regular mail as an authorized method (Tex. Prop. Code §24.005(f)). CA does not.

candidates.facts: The tenant of record is 'Main Street LLC,' a California LLC. The notice is personally delivered to the LLC's registered agent for service of process at the agent's registered address.
candidates.question: Is this valid service on a business entity tenant?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: Service on a business entity is governed by CCP §1162 in conjunction with Corporations Code provisions for service on entities. Delivery to the registered agent at the registered agent's address constitutes valid service. Personal delivery to an authorized agent satisfies CCP §1162(a)(1) for an entity.
candidates.edge_cases: Service at the leased premises on an employee present may also be valid if the employee has authority. DRAFT: registered agent service is the safest method.

candidates.scenario: Notice left under door — no posting on main door, no one home
candidates.facts: Process server slides the notice under the front door of the unit. No mailed copy is sent. Tenant is not home.
candidates.question: Is this valid service?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: Sliding under the door is not an enumerated service method under CCP §1162. It does not constitute 'posting on the main entrance' (nail-and-mail) or personal delivery. Service is void.
candidates.edge_cases: If someone from inside the unit opens the door during the attempt and the server hands the notice through the door — that may convert to personal delivery. Purely under-door sliding: void.

candidates.scenario: Substituted service: left with property manager (not at tenant's unit)
candidates.facts: Tenant is not home. Process server leaves the notice with the building's on-site property manager in the management office (not the tenant's unit). Server mails copy to tenant at the unit address.
candidates.question: Is this valid substituted service?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: CCP §1162(a)(2) requires leaving the notice with a person of suitable age and discretion 'found at the residence.' The management office is not the tenant's residence. Courts are divided on whether leaving notice with property manager at management office (rather than at the unit) satisfies this requirement. DRAFT: likely invalid — flag for attorney.
candidates.edge_cases: If property manager is also resident of the building and was found at or near the unit, result may differ. Key is whether 'residence' means the specific unit or the building generally.

candidates.scenario: Mailed copy time: mailed 5 days after posting (nail-and-mail)
candidates.facts: Process server posts notice on door on June 1. Mails copy on June 6 (5 days later). When does the 3-day notice period begin?
candidates.question: Does the 5-day gap between posting and mailing affect validity or the start of the notice period?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: CCP §1162(a)(3) requires posting and mailing, but does not explicitly require simultaneous mailing. Some courts hold the notice period does not begin until mailing is completed. A 5-day gap between posting and mailing is unusual and may be argued to affect the start of the period. DRAFT: mailing should occur promptly (same day or next day) after posting; significant delay may invalidate or re-start the 3-day period from the mailing date.
candidates.edge_cases: If court holds period begins at mailing (June 6), then 3 days = June 9. Landlord filing UD on June 5 would be premature.

candidates.scenario: Service adds 5 days for mail — when does period expire?
candidates.facts: Notice is served by substituted service (left with adult + mailed) on June 1. Tenant claims the 3-day period doesn't start until 5 days after mailing under CCP §1013.
candidates.question: Does the 5-day extension of CCP §1013 apply to add time after mailed service?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: CCP §1013 extends response time by 5 days when service is by mail. Courts are split on whether this applies to UD notice periods: some hold that the 3-day period under §1161 begins from the mailing date plus 5 days (i.e., 8 days total); others hold that the 3-day period begins at mailing without extension. This is an active area of dispute in CA UD practice.
candidates.edge_cases: This uncertainty significantly affects UD filing timing. Attorney must establish the controlling rule for the target jurisdiction/court.

candidates.scenario: Service on co-tenants: notice served on one of two named tenants
candidates.facts: Two people signed the lease as co-tenants (A and B). Landlord serves the 3-day notice only on A. A and B are both currently in possession.
candidates.question: Must notice be served on both named co-tenants?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: Each named tenant of record must be served with the notice. Serving only co-tenant A does not constitute valid service on co-tenant B. A UD judgment cannot be entered against B without proper service on B. Landlord must serve each co-tenant separately (or serve one and comply with CCP §1162 methods that would reach both).
candidates.edge_cases: If B is not home but A is, personal service on A and substituted service on B (via A) at the premises may be possible in one visit. Check whether A can accept on behalf of B — DRAFT: A is a suitable-age person found at the residence for B's substituted service, but both named tenants should still be listed on the notice.
